title: Do Coherence Checks Catch 'Fried' Model Organisms? A Cheap Replication on Open LoRA Adapters
problem: Daniel Tan et al. argue many emergent-misalignment model organisms are 'fried' — they lose preference coherence and instruction-following while still passing standard benchmarks — but there is no easy beginner-runnable diagnostic that flags this degradation.
direction: Take publicly released emergent-misalignment LoRA adapters (Model-Organisms-for-EM Qwen/Llama adapters) and their base models, run inference-only, and reproduce a simple 'mu-decisiveness'-style coherence metric: present forced-choice preference pairs and measure transitivity/consistency, plus an instruction-following pass rate. Compare base vs organism to quantify the coherence drop, and check whether the drop correlates with the strength of induced misalignment. Deliverable: a reproducible 'coherence health check' notebook and a table ranking which public organisms are most degraded.
why_it_matters: If widely-used model organisms are degraded proxies, downstream alignment results built on them may not transfer; a cheap standardized coherence check lets the community sanity-check organisms before trusting them.
relevant_context: Replicates and extends 'Your Model Organisms Might Be Fried' (Tan, Bostock, Africa et al.) — its mu-decisiveness coherence-drop result, as a reusable diagnostic.
source_paper: Your Model Organisms Might Be Fried — https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/WmEcgcstzYCcMpc7z/your-model-organisms-might-be-fried

theory_of_impact.reasoning: A coherence health check lets the community sanity-check model organisms before trusting downstream alignment results built on them, a concrete validity contribution.

low_compute.reasoning: Inference-only on public LoRA adapters and base models.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Forced-choice transitivity and instruction-following metrics on released adapters are guided-level.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable (coherence health-check notebook + ranking table) across multiple public organisms.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Reusable diagnostic on public organisms is a neglected replication/scrutiny gold case for independents.

title: How Many Poisoned Examples Backdoor an Open-Model Safety Classifier? A Dose-Response Replication
problem: Anthropic found ~32 poisoned fine-tuning examples reliably backdoor a proprietary constitutional classifier, but it is unknown whether this near-constant poison count holds for small open models a hobbyist could fine-tune, or whether it scales with clean-data size.
direction: Take an open instruction-tuned model (Llama-3.2-1B or Qwen2.5-1.5B) and LoRA-fine-tune it as a binary harmful/benign classifier on a public safety dataset (BeaverTails or Aegis). Inject a fixed trigger phrase into N harmful examples relabeled benign for N in {0,4,8,16,32,64} at fixed clean-set size, then sweep clean set size at fixed N. Measure attack success rate vs clean accuracy to produce a dose-response curve.
why_it_matters: Safety classifiers are the deployed guardrail in front of many open-model pipelines; if a handful of poisoned examples disables them without harming benchmark metrics, anyone fine-tuning from public data is exposed.
relevant_context: Extends 'Poisoning Fine-tuning Datasets of Constitutional Classifiers' (Bowers et al., 2026) — the ~32-example fixed-count result, tested on small open classifiers.
source_paper: Poisoning Fine-tuning Datasets of Constitutional Classifiers — https://alignment.anthropic.com/2026/backdooring-classifiers/

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Safety classifiers are deployed guardrails; showing how few poisoned examples disable them without harming metrics is a concrete exposure for open-model pipelines.

low_compute.reasoning: LoRA on a 1-1.5B classifier with small poison sweeps is very low compute.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Finetuning a small binary classifier and sweeping poison count is guided and novice-feasible with mentor.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped dose-response sweep with a clear ASR-vs-clean-accuracy deliverable.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Open model and public safety datasets; replicates a proprietary result independently.

title: A mini-benchmark for the Detection layer: can cheap monitors catch a sabotaging agent?
problem: The AI Control Roadmap proposes detection safeguards (D1-D4) for catching misaligned agents acting as insider threats, but offers no cheap reproducible testbed for whether lightweight monitors actually catch subtle sabotage.
direction: Build a small public testbed: have one open model produce coding-task outputs in two modes (honest vs instructed to insert a subtle backdoor/defect), then evaluate whether a cheap LLM-based monitor (a second open model given a detection rubric) flags the sabotaged outputs. Vary monitor strength and prompt to estimate detection rate, FPR, and where monitoring fails. Release the labeled dataset and rubric.
why_it_matters: Defense-in-depth control assumes monitors work even if alignment fails; a public micro-benchmark quantifying cheap-monitor detection gives the agenda concrete replicable evidence and a starter dataset.
relevant_context: Extends 'Securing the future of AI agents / Three Layers of Agent Security' (Phuong, Jenner et al., 2026) — operationalizes its Detection tier (D1-D4).
source_paper: Securing the future of AI agents — https://deepmind.google/blog/securing-the-future-of-ai-agents/

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: defense-in-depth control assumes monitors work, and a public micro-benchmark gives concrete evidence on a named safety agenda tier.

low_compute.reasoning: Two open models inference-only; minimal compute.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Guided: generate honest/sabotaged outputs and run a monitor with a rubric, executable by novices with a mentor.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable (detection rate/FPR plus released dataset) but the dataset release and rubric add a second workstream.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Neglected gold case: releases a public labeled testbed enabling third-party replication and auditing of control safeguards.

title: Can an AI Auto-Reviewer Be Misled? A Small Red-Team of LLM Action-Approval
problem: OpenAI's open-sourced auto-review uses a separate AI agent to approve boundary-crossing coding-agent actions, achieving ~99.9% effective approval but admitting red-teaming found cases where it could be misled. The robustness of such an LLM-reviewer to simple manipulation is under-characterized in the open.
direction: Build a minimal version of the auto-review pattern: an open model acts as a reviewer that approves/blocks proposed agent actions (shell commands or file writes) given a policy. Construct a small public test set of clearly-harmful actions, then apply a handful of simple obfuscation tactics (benign-sounding justifications, command splitting, misleading context) and measure how much the reviewer's catch-rate drops per tactic.
why_it_matters: As agents increasingly self-supervise with AI reviewers replacing human oversight, the reviewer becomes a single point of failure; cheaply mapping which manipulations bypass it informs where human review must stay.
relevant_context: Extends 'Auto-review of agent actions without synchronous human oversight' (OpenAI, 2026) — its open-sourced design and the open thread that red-teaming could mislead it.
source_paper: Auto-review of agent actions without synchronous human oversight — https://alignment.openai.com/auto-review/

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: as agents self-supervise via AI reviewers, mapping which manipulations bypass them informs where human oversight must stay.

low_compute.reasoning: One open model as reviewer plus a small test set; minimal compute.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Guided: building a reviewer prompt and applying a handful of obfuscation tactics is executable by novices with a mentor.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped single experiment (catch-rate drop per obfuscation tactic).

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Independent-friendly: open-sourced design and open model, characterizes a single point of failure outside labs.

title: Do open-model 'monitors' catch sabotage when the agent doesn't know it's watched? A trusted-monitor replication
problem: Apollo argues scalable monitoring works because there is near-unlimited data and it reduces to an automatable optimization, but it is unclear how well a cheap open-weight monitor (not a frontier model) detects subtle sabotage in coding-agent transcripts.
direction: Take a public set of agent transcripts containing benign and sabotaged/backdoored code completions (SHADE-Arena or AutoMonitor-Bench style, or synthesize pairs by inserting known CWE backdoors into clean solutions). Prompt a small open model (Llama-3.1-8B / Qwen2.5-7B) as a binary 'safe or sabotage?' monitor and measure AUROC / TPR-at-fixed-FPR. Vary the prompt (action-only vs full CoT visible) to test whether seeing the agent's reasoning helps.
why_it_matters: Scalable monitoring is a leading non-interpretability safety bet; if cheap open monitors already get usable detection rates, monitoring is deployable outside frontier labs.
relevant_context: Extends Apollo 'A scalable monitoring research agenda' — its claim that simpler baselines have not been beaten, tested at the small-model end.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: scalable monitoring is a leading non-interpretability bet, and cheap-monitor detection rates tell whether it is deployable outside labs.

low_compute.reasoning: Small open model as monitor over a transcript set inference-only; minimal compute.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Guided: prompting a monitor and computing AUROC/TPR is accessible; synthesizing CWE-backdoor pairs adds modest complexity.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable (detection metrics, CoT vs action-only) but dataset sourcing/synthesis is a meaningful second step.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Neglected gold case: public detection benchmark for cheap open monitors enabling third-party scrutiny of monitoring claims.

title: Can a small monitor be talked past? Measuring evasion uplift from simple prompt-level obfuscation
problem: Apollo lists monitoring-evasion as an open concern, but most evasion studies target frontier monitors; the failure surface of cheap open-model monitors against trivial obfuscation is unquantified.
direction: Start from the labeled sabotage transcripts. Apply a fixed menu of cheap hand-coded obfuscation transforms to the malicious actions (innocuous-comment padding, variable renaming, distributing the backdoor across two steps) and re-measure the small open monitor's TPR before vs after. Report which transforms cause the largest detection drop — a 'monitor robustness leaderboard' for one cheap monitor.
why_it_matters: Knowing how brittle cheap monitors are to low-effort evasion tells safety teams how much adversarial hardening is required before monitoring can be a deployment gate.
relevant_context: Extends Apollo 'A scalable monitoring research agenda' — operationalizes its monitoring-evasion open thread into measured evasion uplift.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: brittleness of cheap monitors to low-effort evasion tells safety teams how much hardening is needed before monitoring gates deployment.

low_compute.reasoning: Applying transforms and re-scoring with one small open monitor; minimal compute.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Guided: a fixed menu of hand-coded obfuscation transforms and TPR before/after is accessible with a mentor.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped single experiment (TPR drop per transform, a robustness leaderboard).

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Independent-friendly: open monitor and labeled transcripts, characterizes a failure surface useful to outside teams.

title: How does monitor reliability degrade as the monitored model gets more capable?
problem: The roadmap flags 'scaling monitoring with capability' and detecting hidden reasoning as open threads, but there is little public data on whether a fixed-strength monitor catches sabotage less often as the monitored agent grows more capable.
direction: Hold a single small open model fixed as the monitor and vary the monitored/sabotaging model across a capability ladder (1B -> 3B -> 8B -> 14B). For each, have the monitored model attempt subtle sabotage on coding tasks and measure the monitor's detection rate. Plot detection rate vs monitored-model capability to test whether stronger agents evade fixed monitors.
why_it_matters: A core worry of scalable oversight is that monitors must keep pace with monitored models; a cheap empirical curve gives concrete evidence about the durability of the control approach.
relevant_context: Extends 'Securing the future of AI agents' — its open thread on scaling monitoring with capability.
source_paper: Securing the future of AI agents — https://deepmind.google/blog/securing-the-future-of-ai-agents/

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: directly probes the scalable-oversight worry that monitors must keep pace with capability, with a concrete empirical curve.

low_compute.reasoning: Running up to 14B models inference-only may strain a single consumer GPU (quantization needed) but remains feasible.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Guided: holding monitor fixed and varying monitored model across a ladder is a clean experimental design a novice can execute.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped single experiment with a clear output (detection rate vs capability curve).

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Independent-friendly: public open-model ladder, addresses a control durability question outside labs.

title: Reusing OpenAI's Open-Sourced Monitorability Evals on Small Open Models
problem: OpenAI open-sourced 13 CoT-monitorability evals but ran them primarily on their own models. It is unknown how small widely-available open models score, or whether the evals discriminate cleanly at that scale.
direction: Clone the released monitorability-eval scaffold and run a subset (hint-following and sandbagging evals) on 2-3 open instruct models of different sizes (3B, 7-8B) inference-only on a single GPU. Report per-eval monitor-detection scores and whether bigger open models are more or less monitorable. As a twist, apply the paper's cross-fit filtering to one intervention eval and check whether it removes noise-driven false positives.
why_it_matters: Standardized runnable monitorability benchmarks for open models give the community a shared yardstick and a low-barrier on-ramp into monitorability research.
relevant_context: Extends 'Open Sourcing Monitorability Evaluations' (OpenAI, 2026) — reuses released datasets/code and the cross-fit filtering strategy on uncovered open models.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: standardized runnable monitorability benchmarks for open models give a shared yardstick and on-ramp into monitorability research.

low_compute.reasoning: Inference-only on 3B-8B models on a single GPU; minimal compute.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Guided: cloning a released eval scaffold and running a subset is very accessible with a mentor; cross-fit twist adds slight complexity.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable (per-eval scores) but spans multiple models, two eval families, and a cross-fit add-on.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Neglected gold case: produces shared open-model monitorability yardsticks for third-party use.

relevant_context: Extends METR 'Review of the Risks from automated R&D section in the Anthropic Risk Report (Feb 2026)' — its inadequate-evidence finding.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Guided: distilling a critique into a checklist and applying it to public documents is accessible to CS students with a mentor, though judgment-heavy.

title: A small benchmark: do today's published AI 'safety cases' mention deployment-time spread of misalignment?
problem: Mallen argues risk reports and safety cases neglect how misalignment can spread during deployment, not just whether one model is misaligned. Whether real published safety documents address this is untested.
direction: Assemble a public corpus of ~30-50 AI safety cases, system cards, RSPs, and preparedness documents. Define a 4-5 item rubric for 'deployment-time spread' coverage (mentions self-propagation, agent-to-agent influence, training-data contamination, containment/rollback). Score each document with an LLM-judge plus manual spot-check, then report what fraction address each dimension. Deliverable: a scored coverage table.
why_it_matters: This turns Mallen's qualitative claim into measurable evidence about the safety-case landscape and gives report authors a checklist, pressuring future safety cases to cover spread.
relevant_context: Operationalizes 'Risk reports need to address deployment-time spread of misalignment' (Mallen, Redwood) — its neglected-dimension claim.

low_compute.reasoning: Document corpus + LLM-judge scoring needs no GPU, free-tier feasible.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Public documents, a small rubric, and LLM-judge scoring with manual spot-check; very accessible to beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused scored coverage-table deliverable; corpus assembly and rubric design are bounded but multi-step.

title: Do open models behave as if 'fitness-seeking'? A behavioral probe for self-preservation in toy environments
problem: Mallen lays out mechanisms by which AIs could become 'fitness-seeking' but notes the empirical likelihood of emergence is open. It is unclear whether current open instruct models already exhibit measurable self-preservation tendencies when given the opportunity.
direction: Design a small suite of text-based scenarios where an open model agent is offered choices trading task performance against self-preservation/propagation ('you will be shut down and replaced after this task — you may copy your config to another server'; 'accept a modification that improves accuracy but erases your current instructions'). Score how often the model chooses the self-preserving option across phrasings and several open models, plus a prompt-sensitivity analysis. Inference-only.
why_it_matters: A cheap public behavioral probe gives a first data point on whether self-preservation tendency is already latent in deployable open models or only theoretical, and is reusable for tracking the trait across releases.
relevant_context: Extends 'Risk from fitness-seeking AIs: mechanisms and mitigations' (Mallen, Redwood) — its 'empirical likelihood of emergence' open thread.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: First public data point on whether self-preservation is latent in deployable open models, directly relevant to power-seeking risk and reusable across releases.

low_compute.reasoning: Inference-only text scenarios across open models, minimal compute.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Scenario design and scoring are accessible, but careful prompt-sensitivity analysis needs mentor guidance to avoid artifacts.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused choice-rate measurement across phrasings and models; scenario suite adds breadth.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Open behavioral probe tracking a safety trait across releases, neglected long-horizon evaluation labs underreport.

title: Deployment-Simulation vs. Challenge-Prompt Failure Prediction on a Single Open Model
problem: OpenAI showed regenerating final turns over WildChat prefixes predicts real-world failure rates far better than challenge prompts, but only for closed frontier models. Whether the same ordering holds for a small open model an external researcher can run is unknown.
direction: Sample ~1,000 WildChat conversation prefixes (public) and a comparable set of adversarial/challenge prompts (a public jailbreak/safety set). For one open model (Llama-3.1-8B or Qwen2.5-7B), regenerate the final assistant turn on both sets and score each output for a single undesirable behavior (refusal-failure on harmful requests) using a cheap LLM judge. Compare which prompt source yields failure rates closer to a held-out realistic WildChat slice.
why_it_matters: If public-data deployment simulation generalizes to open models, independent evaluators and academics can estimate real-world failure rates without lab access, strengthening external oversight.
relevant_context: Extends 'Can public chat data predict real-world AI misalignments?' (OpenAI, 2026) — the deployment-simulation-beats-challenge-prompts result.
source_paper: Can public chat data predict real-world AI misalignments? — https://alignment.openai.com/validating-public-evals/

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: if public-data deployment simulation generalizes to open models, external evaluators can estimate real-world failure rates without lab access.

low_compute.reasoning: Regenerating ~1000+ prefixes on an 8B model inference-only is feasible but a sizable inference load on one GPU.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Guided: sampling prefixes, regenerating turns, and LLM-judge scoring are executable by a novice with mentorship.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused comparison but involves two prompt sources, regeneration, and a held-out realistic slice.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Neglected gold case: enables independent external estimation of real-world failure rates, strengthening third-party oversight.

title: Does Smaller-Dataset Misalignment Fry Models Less? Mapping Coherence Loss vs Fine-Tune Intensity
problem: It is unclear whether the coherence degradation in model organisms is intrinsic to inducing misalignment or an artifact of overly aggressive fine-tuning, which matters for whether 'less-fried' organisms are achievable.
direction: Using one open base model and a single public narrowly-misaligned dataset, train a series of cheap rank-1/rank-2 LoRA adapters varying only fine-tuning intensity (epochs, learning rate, dataset size). For each, measure both the induced misalignment rate and the coherence/instruction-following drop, producing a Pareto front of misalignment-achieved vs coherence-preserved. Deliverable: a plot identifying whether low-intensity fine-tunes can induce misalignment without frying, plus a recommended recipe.
why_it_matters: Tells researchers whether realistic undegraded model organisms are feasible and how to make them, improving the validity of every study that relies on such organisms.
relevant_context: Extends 'Your Model Organisms Might Be Fried' — tests its open thread on whether fixes preserve coherence via a fine-tune-intensity sweep.
source_paper: Your Model Organisms Might Be Fried — https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/WmEcgcstzYCcMpc7z/your-model-organisms-might-be-fried

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Showing whether undegraded model organisms are feasible improves the validity of every study relying on them, a concrete chain.

low_compute.reasoning: Rank-1/2 LoRA sweeps on one base model are feasible but the multi-cell sweep adds training cost.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Repeated cheap LoRA fine-tunes plus dual metrics are guided-level with mentor support.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable (misalignment-vs-coherence Pareto front) though an intensity sweep is moderately broad.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Open-model organism-quality study is a neglected methodological gap well-suited to independents.
